label: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries

cards.front: When deciding which tool to call, what information does Claude have access to?
cards.back: Only the name, description, and parameter schema you provide. Claude has no access to your implementation, intent, or mental model — design descriptions like API docs for someone who can't ask follow-up questions.

cards.front: What three questions must a tool description answer unambiguously?
cards.back: 1) What does this tool do? (purpose, not implementation) 2) When should it be used? (the trigger/condition) 3) What does it NOT do? (its explicit boundary). The third is often omitted but most important for disambiguation.

cards.front: How does Claude select which tool to call, and why does a vague description hurt?
cards.back: Claude matches the user's goal against the semantic content of each description. A vague description causes Claude to guess; a precise one causes correct selection every time.

cards.front: When two tools handle related but distinct concerns, how should their descriptions be written?
cards.back: Make the distinction explicit — even if it feels redundant. E.g., 'get_user_by_id: retrieve a single user by exact UUID' vs. 'search_users: search by name/email/role, returns a list.' Include 'Do NOT use this for X' boundaries.

cards.front: List the conditions that indicate you should SPLIT one tool into multiple tools.
cards.back: Split when: two actions have different preconditions or risk profiles (read vs. write); conflating requires complex parameter logic (mode: get|search); or one action is safe to call speculatively while the other has side effects.

cards.front: List the conditions that indicate you should CONSOLIDATE operations into one tool.
cards.back: Consolidate when: operations are always performed together with no independent use; splitting creates artificial back-and-forth (two round-trips for one logical step); or the distinction would only confuse routing without improving precision.

cards.front: Why is a mode/action parameter (e.g. action: 'get' | 'list' | 'delete') an exam trap?
cards.back: It's a strong signal the tool should be split. A mode parameter switching between fundamentally different behaviors turns one tool into several with a single confusing entry point — each action should get its own description and selection logic.

cards.front: What are the best practices for parameter naming and schema design in tool interfaces?
cards.back: Name parameters for their semantic role, not data type (userId not id, startDate not date1); state expected format in the description ('ISO 8601 date, e.g. 2024-01-15'); mark optional params and explain omission effects; enumerate valid values inline when the set is small and fixed.

cards.front: Why is 'leaking implementation details' in a tool description a common mistake?
cards.back: Descriptions like 'calls the /v2/invoices/{id} endpoint' describe the mechanism, not the purpose. Claude needs semantic meaning to select correctly, not internal implementation details.

cards.front: What is the danger of over-consolidating read and write operations into one tool?
cards.back: Claude cannot reliably distinguish safe from destructive calls when they share a single description. Combining read/write just because they touch the same resource makes it impossible to route safely — split them so each has its own boundary.
